It doesn't scale super well, because beyond a certain point AI has no taste, and the training data is short. So the dev has to instruct it more and more.

The early stages come down to "make a game like X" on a loop gauntlet. Then it does it. Going beyond is rapidly diminishing returns with current tech, requiring game design sense, etc.

replies.author: TopTippityTop
replies.body:
It's possible to make personal projects right now. The issue is that these games you see are highly present in the training data. Making an original game would require 1. Knowing what you want to build. 2. Knowing it's actually a good idea (most are not). 3. Knowing how to make it good (AI won't know. It'll need direction. It just know what fun is, it just knows what's in the data. You have to direct it step by step towards that fun. 4. Getting to fun is often a matter of precisely calibrated balance. Often times it requires things which don't jibe with common sense, such as the most obvious one... Removing realism. These mean tools, very specific tools. AI can make the tools, but the dev needs to know why.

Ultimately AI has made no improvements in actual game design. It has improved on production value and coding, but still fails at: good concept art. Good engineering (architecture, etc). Game design. 

Because these require taste, and taste isn't easily found in data. Taste adapts to the occasion, and is learned through experience over a lot of trials and errors. Heck, even a lot of game designers don't have it (why many games end up looking good but being boring). 
 
Design for concept art is a bit tough, but not impossible to solve. It requires a sense of real art direction, market research, understanding of themes, iconography, symbolism, motifs. An understanding of what humans find interesting and engaging + how it fits with design goals + how colors affect humans, readability for different types of pov/experiences, etc. A real sense of design. Then it'll go beyond the "pretty image stage" it's at now.


So what we will have soon is a whole bunch of somewhat generic (or unique but... Strange) looking AAA production quality games, fairly overengineered and bug prone, that aren't fun for more than the time it takes for the initial excitement to wear off.

However, there will be games which are easier to design, or require skills that many may have without needing to have gone through a game dev experience, such as narrative based games, puzzle games, etc. Even fps isn't extremely hard to design, so we may see a few decent ones. Realism will be MUCH easier.

I predict many others will remain pretty sloppy for a while, until AI learns taste, and all the qualities which aren't easily put into words. We'll probably get there, but there's been basically no progress on it.... Probably due to the fact that llms are primarily trained on words. As they become more multi modal and contain deeper world models + have enough gama analytics and balance data, it's possible they'll start getting better at those aspects.
